Oji Udezue (00:31:34):
Yeah, I feel like all of park management is about discovery these days. Everyone talks about it, and I want to make a distinction. I think discovery is when you use customer conversations to understand a very specific thing that you want to optimize further workflow that you want to optimize further. There's a version of that also that is what I call continuous conversations, which is a Calendly and a Typeform, which we'll do more and more of. You should organize it so that your PMs, your designers, your engineering managers and your PMMs are constantly talking to customers by default. Meaning that customer conversations show up on their calendar every week automagically, without them getting involved. And then they're trained on how to have the conversation, because the death of customer discovery is friction. If you ask individuals to do customer discovery, they will not do customer discovery.

answer.summary: To find customers, set up interviews consistently, and conduct them, Zoelle Egner recommends writing a template email for yourself that you can send out easily, thanking the recipient for using the product, and asking for their experience and feedback. She also suggests setting up a hypothesis of the type of person you want to talk to and running a query against your database to find someone to send three emails a week. Dalton Caldwell advises that overcoming social anxiety and awkwardness when talking to customers requires getting past the feeling of looking stupid and starting to do it until it doesn't feel bad anymore. He also suggests setting up a system to talk to customers, such as having 20-30% of your time dedicated to customer meetings, and that nothing substitutes for an actual conversation versus just staring at analytics dashboards.

sections.content: Dalton Caldwell advises that overcoming social anxiety and awkwardness when talking to customers requires getting past the feeling of looking stupid and starting to do it until it doesn't feel bad anymore. He also suggests setting up a system to talk to customers, such as having 20-30% of your time dedicated to customer meetings, and that nothing substitutes for an actual conversation versus just staring at analytics dashboards.
